newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Commonwealth wants to save debtors, outwit crooks.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth wants to save debtors, outwit crooks.

text.p: International proposals to bail out the world's poorest debtor nations will come under attack for not going far enough when finance ministers from the Commonwealth meet here this week.

Ministers, representing most of the 53 members of the former British Empire which makes up the Commonwealth, will also look at how to stamp out money-laundering and encourage instead the inflow of legitimate private capital to prime their economies.

"We want to see how to get proposals on terms for debt relief improved. Terms are too tough for seriously indebted countries," Commonwealth Secretary General Humphrey Maude told reporters ahead of the September 24-26 talks in this Caribbean island.
All but five of the countries in the group are classed as developing economies, ranging from Asian giant India to tiny islands in the Pacific and Caribbean.
Many are struggling to pay off huge debts, including to multilateral financial institutions like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Commonwealth officials described the meeting as the one chance each year when developing members can join with leading economies such as Britain and Canada to lobby the international community on their behalf.
"We expect quite a tough debate...we hope for consensus on easing (debt relief) terms," Maude said.

Their views will be taken on to Washington the following week to the annual IMF/World Bank meeting in Washington where debt relief will figure high on the agenda, including the deeply contentious question of whether to use some of the IMF's gold.

Up to 20 of the world's poorest countries have been targetted as in urgent need of help but officials say in reality only two or three countries can expect quick help to pull them out of a deepening debt trap.

The Commonwealth's chief concerns are that it is too difficult for many of the most needy to meet the terms for debt relief, that it takes too long for the help to arrive and that the burden for providing assistance is not fairly shared out.
Commonwealth officials said they realised that it was equally important for the countries themselves to prove that they were making serious attempts to put their own economies on track.

Ministers will look at ways to bring in more private investment to offset "aid fatigue" which has seen aid to developing countries slide as industrial nations focus more on how to slash their own budget deficits.

That includes how to deal with the surge of flows in and out of an economy, which was held responsible for the near catastrophe that hit Mexico's economy one and a half years ago, and whose effects are still swirling the world of international finance.

On the other side of the coin, the Commonwealth will press ahead with efforts to prevent illicit money coming through member countries -- several of them international tax havens -- which are used to launder to earnings of drug dealers and their like.
However, officials concede that several are reluctant to do anything that would also limit banking secrecy in case it scares off more legitimate investment.
